scenes.title: A cyclist climbs and speeds up

beats.text: Consider a cyclist riding a bicycle uphill. Watch the whole journey first. The cyclist pedals from the lower point towards the higher point, gaining speed along the way.
At the upper point, the cyclist is higher and moving faster. We will treat the cyclist and bicycle as one system, with a constant total mass.
Freeze the journey into two snapshots. Now let us state the complete question.
beats.caption: Two snapshots of the same journey

scenes.title: The complete question
scenes.source: Recording38–53 original mass question; PDF9–11 height extension

beats.text: At point A, the cyclist and bicycle have an initial speed of four metres per second.
At point B, their final speed is eight metres per second.
They have climbed three metres vertically. Choose A as the zero height datum. This is the change in height, not the distance along the road.
During this journey, their kinetic energy increases by two point four kilojoules.
Take g as ten metres per second squared, constant throughout. Model the cyclist and bicycle as a single particle of constant total mass.
Find the total mass of the cyclist and bicycle, and the gain in gravitational potential energy from A to B. Both unknowns are on our diagram. Take a moment to read the whole question.

scenes.title: Kinetic energy: final minus initial

beats.text: Kinetic energy is energy associated with motion. For mass m and speed v, kinetic energy equals one half m v squared.
Energy is a scalar: it has no direction. Use speed, the magnitude of velocity. Squaring speed makes kinetic energy nonnegative. A stationary object has no kinetic energy.
beats.caption: KE is nonnegative; speed has no direction

beats.text: For this journey, u names the initial speed and v the final speed. Write the change as final kinetic energy minus initial kinetic energy.
The mass stays constant, so factor out one half m. We get one half m, multiplied by v squared minus u squared.
Notice what is inside the brackets. Square each speed first, then subtract. Do not subtract the speeds and square that difference. Those are different expressions.
beats.caption: Square each speed, then subtract

beats.text: Speeding up gives a positive change. Slowing down would give a negative change, even though the kinetic energy itself remains nonnegative.
beats.caption: KE ≥ 0; its change can be negative

scenes.title: Use the energy change to find mass

beats.text: Now use that formula to find the unknown mass. Change in kinetic energy equals one half m times final speed squared minus initial speed squared.
Our energy increase is in kilojoules. One kilojoule is one thousand joules, so convert before substituting.
Two point four kilojoules therefore becomes two thousand four hundred joules.
Substitute the increase of two thousand four hundred joules, the final speed of eight, and the initial speed of four. The mass is still unknown.
Eight squared is sixty four; four squared is sixteen. We subtract these squared speeds.
Sixty four minus sixteen is forty eight. Half of forty eight is twenty four, so two thousand four hundred equals twenty four m.
Divide both sides by twenty four. The total mass is one hundred kilograms.
That is the mass of the cyclist and bicycle together. Put it back on the diagram: we need this same mass for the height part of the question.

scenes.title: Gravitational potential energy
scenes.source: Explicit PDF9–11 bridge, absent from recording

beats.text: Now consider height. Gravitational potential energy depends on an object’s vertical height relative to a chosen datum. It equals mass times g times height.
The dashed line through A is our datum. Its height is zero. B is three metres vertically above it. The road length is irrelevant to this calculation.
The cyclist does not have to stop to possess gravitational potential energy. While moving above the datum, the cyclist has both kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy.
With mass and g constant, the change in gravitational potential energy equals m g times the change in vertical height.
Final height minus initial height is three minus zero, giving a rise of three metres.
Substitute our total mass of one hundred kilograms, g of ten, and a vertical rise of three metres.
This gives three thousand joules. The positive change means a gain in gravitational potential energy.
Choosing a different datum changes the individual heights and potential energies. It does not change the vertical rise, or the gain we just found.

scenes.title: What would change on a descent?
scenes.source: PDF9–11 signed changes; recording30–38; no extra numerical problem

beats.text: Imagine the same system later descends. We are changing the direction of the height change; we are not assuming how its speed changes.
Its final height would be lower than its initial height. Final minus initial is negative, so its gravitational potential energy decreases.
A loss of gravitational potential energy means a negative change. It does not tell us by itself whether the cyclist is speeding up or slowing down.
beats.caption: Downhill: Δh < 0, so ΔGPE < 0

beats.text: Suppose the cyclist is moving above our datum. Must its gravitational potential energy be zero just because it is moving? Think about it.
beats.caption: Moving above the datum: is GPE zero?

beats.text: No. Height gives gravitational potential energy, and motion gives kinetic energy. Both can be present at the same time.
beats.caption: Moving and above datum: both KE and GPE
